title: Kassiano et al. 2023 — Systematic review: ROM effects on muscle hypertrophy (Which ROMs Lead to Rome?)
text: Kassiano et al. systematically reviewed 11 studies on range of motion and muscle hypertrophy. Full ROM and partial ROM in the initial (lengthened) portion elicited greater hypertrophy of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, biceps brachii, and brachialis distal sites compared to partial ROM in the final (shortened) portion (effect sizes d = 0.20-0.90). Partial ROM at the middle of ROM elicited greater triceps brachii hypertrophy than full ROM (d = 1.21). The key finding: when training at a longer muscle length — through either partial ROM or full ROM — some muscles experience optimal growth. Combining initial-ROM (lengthened) partials with full ROM should be prioritized. Practical coaching application: prioritize exercises that train muscles in their stretched/lengthened position. For quads: deep squats or hack squat at bottom. For biceps: incline curls. For triceps: overhead extensions. The shortened partial (top half only) is the least effective strategy.

title: Kassiano et al. 2023 — RCT: gastrocnemius hypertrophy from training at long muscle lengths
text: Kassiano et al. conducted an RCT with 42 young women comparing three calf raise ROM groups: full ROM, initial ROM (ankle at dorsiflexion/lengthened), and final ROM (plantarflexion/shortened). Key findings: initial ROM (lengthened) produced +15.2% medial gastrocnemius thickness vs +6.7% full ROM and +3.4% final ROM (p ≤ 0.009). Lateral gastrocnemius: initial ROM +14.9% vs final ROM +6.2% (p < 0.024). The 8-week protocol used 3 sets of 15-20 RM, 3x/week. Practical coaching application: for calf training, perform standing or leg-press calf raises through the bottom/stretched range (deep dorsiflexion stretch). The commonly practiced 'squeeze at the top' partial movement produces far less hypertrophy. Emphasize the stretch phase.

title: Pedrosa et al. 2022 — RCT: partial ROM at long muscle lengths favors quad hypertrophy
sample: 45 untrained women, 5 groups including Full ROM, Initial ROM, Final ROM, Varied ROM, Control
text: Pedrosa et al. conducted an RCT with 45 women comparing 5 groups for knee extension. The initial ROM group (100-65 degrees of knee flexion = lengthened quad position) produced greater relative CSA increases at 70% femur length vs all other groups including Full ROM. The final ROM group (shortened quad) showed similar changes to the no-training control at 60% and 70% femur length. Varied ROM (alternating daily) showed similar 1RM increases regardless of ROM tested — best for strength transfer. Co-authored by Brad Schoenfeld. Practical coaching application: knee extension performed through the bottom range (lengthened quad) is superior for regional hypertrophy. For strength development across angles, varied ROM programming (alternating ranges daily) is optimal.

title: Maeo et al. 2023 — RCT: triceps hypertrophy substantially greater in overhead vs neutral position
text: Maeo et al. used a contralateral within-subject design (21 adults, 12 weeks, 2x/week) to compare overhead arm position (triceps long head stretched/lengthened) vs neutral arm position (shortened) for elbow extensions at 70% 1RM. Results: triceps long head grew +28.5% (overhead) vs +19.6% (neutral) — 1.5-fold greater (d = 0.61, p < 0.001). Total triceps brachii: +19.9% vs +13.9% (d = 0.54, p < 0.001). Critically, these results occurred even though absolute loads were 34-39% LOWER in the overhead condition. Confirmed by MRI muscle volume measurements. Practical coaching application: always include overhead triceps work (overhead cable extension, French press, overhead DB extension) in programs targeting triceps mass. The stretched position is the active mechanism — you don't need to go as heavy.

title: Schoenfeld et al. 2016 — RCT: longer interset rest periods enhance strength and hypertrophy
sample: 21 resistance-trained men, 8 weeks, 3x/week (SHORT: 1-min n=10; LONG: 3-min n=11)
text: Schoenfeld et al. conducted the landmark RCT comparing 1-minute vs 3-minute rest intervals in 21 resistance-trained men over 8 weeks. The LONG (3-min) group showed significantly greater 1RM squat AND bench press gains than SHORT (1-min). LONG also produced significantly greater anterior thigh (quad) hypertrophy by ultrasound, with a trend toward greater triceps hypertrophy (p=0.06). Both groups increased upper body muscular endurance equally. This study directly debunked the old belief that short rest equals more hypertrophy via metabolic stress. Practical coaching application: for trained lifters targeting both strength and hypertrophy, 2-3 minute rest intervals are superior to 1 minute. The metabolic stress hypothesis for hypertrophy does not hold up longitudinally. Rest more to grow more.

title: Bernárdez-Vázquez et al. 2022 — Umbrella review: RT variables for muscle hypertrophy optimization
text: Bernárdez-Vázquez et al. conducted an umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses (178 primary studies, 4,784 participants) on RT variables for muscle hypertrophy. Key findings: eccentric contractions are important for hypertrophy. Very slow repetitions (≥10 seconds total) should be avoided — excessive time under tension does not enhance hypertrophy and reduces load capacity. Minimum ≥10 sets/week per muscle group is optimal. BFR was cited as beneficial for specific populations. Exercise order and time of day do NOT directly influence magnitude of hypertrophic gains. Practical coaching application: optimal tempo is 2-4s eccentric, 1-2s concentric. Don't use excessively slow tempos (10s+) as they're counterproductive. Prioritize controlled eccentrics with meaningful loads rather than artificially slowing every rep.

title: Križaj et al. 2022 — Umbrella review: chronic effects of eccentric exercise across populations
text: Križaj et al. synthesized 35 systematic reviews on chronic eccentric exercise effects. Key findings: eccentric exercise improved muscle performance (strength, power) across populations. It improved muscle architecture: pennation angle, fascicle length, CSA, and muscle thickness. Eccentric contractions produce lower metabolic demand per unit of force, making eccentric-emphasis training attractive for clinical/rehab populations. Eccentric contractions can produce force up to 130% of maximal concentric force. Effective for pain reduction in musculoskeletal conditions (tendinopathy, DOMS adaptation). Risk of muscle damage with high eccentric loads warrants progressive overload principles. Practical coaching application: eccentric overload techniques (slow negatives, eccentrics-only reps) can be periodically incorporated for novel stimulus in advanced trainees. Particularly useful for tendon health and injury prevention. Start conservative — eccentric training causes more DOMS initially.

title: Lixandrão et al. 2018 — Meta-analysis: BFR vs high-load RT for hypertrophy and strength
sample: Multiple RCTs, systematic review and meta-analysis (PEDro score ≥4)
text: Lixandrão et al. conducted the foundational meta-analysis comparing high-load resistance training (>65% 1RM) to low-load BFR training (<50% 1RM). Key findings: muscle hypertrophy was SIMILAR between HL-RT and BFR-RT regardless of occlusion pressure or cuff width. However, muscle STRENGTH gains were GREATER with HL-RT. BFR-RT is a valid and effective approach for increasing muscle strength across a wide spectrum of ages, particularly for individuals with physical limitations preventing heavy loading. Practical coaching application: BFR is a legitimate tool for hypertrophy when you can't train heavy (travel, deload, post-injury, early rehab). Use 20-40% 1RM with arterial occlusion at 40-80%. Don't expect it to outperform heavy training for strength, but muscle growth is comparable.

title: Davids et al. 2021 — RCT: BFR activates same molecular pathways as heavy training in trained individuals
sample: 21 trained males and females (4.9 ± 2.6 years experience), 9 weeks, 3x/week
text: Davids et al. conducted an RCT comparing low-load BFR vs high-load RT in 21 experienced resistance trainers (4.9 ± 2.6 years training) over 9 weeks. Key findings: quadricep CSA increased similarly — BFR +7.4% vs HL-RT +4.6% (p=0.37, not significant). Muscular strength: HL-RT showed superior squat 1RM gains (p < 0.01). Importantly, acute signaling via mTOR/S6K1 phosphorylation and ribosomal RNA transcription factors were SIMILAR between BFR and HL-RT — first mechanistic evidence in trained individuals. This validates BFR beyond untrained/clinical populations. Practical coaching application: BFR activates the same molecular hypertrophy pathways as heavy training even in experienced lifters. Use during deload weeks (reducing joint stress while maintaining hypertrophic stimulus), during travel without heavy equipment, or for accumulation phases targeting volume without fatigue.

title: Moesgaard et al. 2022 — Meta-analysis: periodization effects on strength and hypertrophy
text: Moesgaard et al. conducted a meta-analysis of 35 volume-equated studies comparing periodized vs non-periodized training. Key findings: periodized training was superior to non-periodized for 1RM strength (ES 0.31, 95% CI [0.04, 0.57], p=0.02). NO difference between periodized and non-periodized for muscle hypertrophy (ES 0.13, p=0.27). Undulating periodization (UP) was superior to linear periodization (LP) for 1RM strength (ES 0.31, p=0.04). Critically, this UP advantage was ONLY present in TRAINED individuals (ES 0.61 in trained; ES 0.06 in untrained). Periodization effects on strength are likely neurophysiological, not hypertrophic. Practical coaching application: for hypertrophy, the specific periodization model doesn't matter — volume and progressive overload are key. For strength in trained athletes, undulating periodization outperforms linear. Use a hybrid: block phases with undulating variation within each block.

title: Keating et al. 2017 — Meta-analysis: HIIT vs MICT on body adiposity
topic: HIIT vs steady-state for fat loss
text: Keating et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies comparing HIIT/SIT to MICT for body fat reduction. Within-group: both significantly reduce body fat % — HIIT -1.26% (95% CI -1.80 to -0.72); MICT -1.48% (95% CI -1.89 to -1.06). Between-group: NO significant difference between HIIT and MICT for any body fat outcome. Analyses comparing MICT vs lower-time-commitment HIIT protocols tended to favor MICT for total body fat (p=0.09). Neither short-term HIIT nor MICT produced clinically meaningful fat reductions alone (effect sizes were modest). Practical coaching application: HIIT is not a fat-loss magic bullet over steady-state when calories burned are equalized. Both produce modest fat loss. HIIT's real advantage is time-efficiency and cardiovascular fitness (VO2max), not superior fat loss per se. Diet remains the primary fat-loss tool.

title: Chen et al. 2024 — Network meta-analysis: exercise types for visceral fat reduction (84 RCTs)
text: Chen et al. conducted the most comprehensive network meta-analysis (84 RCTs, 4,836 participants) on exercise types and visceral adipose tissue. All modalities reduced VAT: aerobic exercise, resistance training, combined AE+RT, and HIIT. SUCRA rankings: vigorous-intensity aerobic + HIIT have the highest probability of being BEST for VAT, weight, total body fat, BMI, waist circumference, and subcutaneous fat. Resistance training was the LEAST effective standalone intervention for VAT reduction. Subgroup finding: RT improved VAT in males and those with body fat <40%, but NOT in females or those with body fat ≥40%. Practical coaching application: for clients targeting visceral fat and metabolic health (the most dangerous fat type), HIIT and vigorous aerobic work are most effective. Pure resistance training alone is weakest for VAT. Combination programming (RT + HIIT) is optimal for overweight/obese clients.
